# Java deserialization of HTTP request data

`qualor:java/unsafe-deserialization` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-502](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/502.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A08_2025-Software_or_Data_Integrity_Failures/), [A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A08_2021-Software_and_Data_Integrity_Failures/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data read with Java serialization: `readObject()` (and similar reads) on an
`ObjectInputStream` or `XMLDecoder` created over request data in the same method, and the
`SerializationUtils` wrappers of Apache Commons Lang and Spring. The request data may be the body
of a servlet request, an uploaded file, or the raw body of a Spring MVC or Jakarta REST handler.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
Java deserialization creates objects of whatever classes the stream names, and runs their
`readObject` and related methods while doing so. With the right classes on the class path
("gadget chains", common in widely used libraries), a crafted stream runs code on the server.
`XMLDecoder` goes further: its XML can call any method directly.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the request body is read as a serialized object.

```java
package com.example.cart;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.ObjectInputStream;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;

public class CartServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws IOException {
        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(request.getInputStream())) {
            Cart cart = (Cart) in.readObject();
            response.setStatus(cart.isEmpty() ? 204 : 200);
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            response.sendError(400);
        }
    }
}
```

**Compliant:** a filter allows only the expected classes, and is set before the first read.

```java
package com.example.cart;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.ObjectInputFilter;
import java.io.ObjectInputStream;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;

public class CartServlet extends HttpServlet {
    private static final ObjectInputFilter CART_ONLY =
            ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter("com.example.cart.Cart;java.base/*;!*");

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws IOException {
        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(request.getInputStream())) {
            in.setObjectInputFilter(CART_ONLY);
            Cart cart = (Cart) in.readObject();
            response.setStatus(cart.isEmpty() ? 204 : 200);
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            response.sendError(400);
        }
    }
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Accept a data format bound to a fixed type instead, such as JSON with Jackson
  (`mapper.readValue(body, Cart.class)`).
- If serialized objects must be read, set an `ObjectInputFilter` that allows only the expected
  classes (`setObjectInputFilter`, before the first read), or use Commons IO
  `ValidatingObjectInputStream` with the accepted classes.
- Never give `XMLDecoder` untrusted input.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Jakarta Servlet
- Spring MVC
- Jakarta REST (JAX-RS)
- Java serialization (ObjectInputStream)
- java.beans.XMLDecoder

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- A handler parameter without an annotation is not a source, except the raw body (an `InputStream`
  or `Reader` parameter, a Spring `HttpEntity` or `RequestEntity`); a Spring `MultipartFile`
  without an annotation (`@RequestParam` or `@RequestPart`) is missed.
- Only a stream created as `ObjectInputStream` or `XMLDecoder` in the same method is followed; one
  opened by a helper is missed. A named subclass of `ObjectInputStream` is never reported, and an
  anonymous subclass counts as safe when its `resolveClass` throws, even if it rejects only a few
  named classes (a deny-list, which OWASP advises against).
- A filter is recognised only when `setObjectInputFilter` is called on the stream before the read
  in the same method; a JVM-wide filter (`ObjectInputFilter.Config.setSerialFilter`, the
  `jdk.serialFilter` property) is not seen.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/java/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.java`](../../../rules/java/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.java) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.

The rule: [`rules/java/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.yml`](../../../rules/java/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.yml), added in version 2026.10.1.
